d: Beams create a visual, animatable effect between two attachments.
h:
A Beam is an object that renders a Texture between two Attachment objects. By setting beam properties, you can:

  • Add a texture and color gradient to create interesting visuals like waterfalls and force fields.
  • Modify a beam's transparency so that it fades over time.
  • Warp its shape by changing the width or curve of each attachment point.
  • Specify the texture's length and mode to affect how it repeats across the beam's length.

Create beams

Before you begin to create a beam, it's useful to toggle on visibility of attachments so you can see where the beam starts and ends. You can do so by enabling Show Constraint Details from Studio's View menu.

To create a beam:

  1. Create two parts and position them a short distance from each other. One will act as the start of the beam and the other as the end of the beam. Group the parts into a Model.

  2. In the Explorer window, add an Attachment object to each part:

  3. Hover over one part and click the ⊕ button. A contextual menu displays.

  4. From the contextual menu, insert an Attachment.

  5. Repeat for the other part.

  6. In the Explorer window, add a Beam object to the model:

  7. Hover over the model and click the ⊕ button. A contextual menu displays.

  8. From the contextual menu, insert a Beam.

  9. Select the new Beam object and assign its attachments. Ensure you assign each attachment property to a different Attachment object.

  10. In the Properties window, select the Attachment0 property. Your cursor changes.

  11. In the Explorer window, select the attachment of the part you want to be the start of your beam.
  12. Back in the Properties window, select the Attachment1 property. Your cursor changes.
  13. In the Explorer window, select the attachment of the part you want to be the end of your beam.

Beams require attachments to function properly. If you remove either attachment object from step 4, the beam stops rendering its texture.

Customize beams

By experimenting with the following properties, you can customize a beam's visual appearance to make unique gameplay elements like force fields, waterfalls, and pathway obstacles.

The visual quality of your beams can change depending on the graphics settings on the player's device. To review your beam across quality levels, it's recommended to open Studio Settings, search for Editor Quality Level, and set it to the both the lowest and highest level after you finish customizing your beam.

Texture

The Texture property renders that texture across the length of the beam. You can set a beam's Texture property to any asset ID. For more information, including how to add or upload your own textures, see here.

A beam renders its texture using two triangles drawn between Segments, and the segments are laid out between the two attachment points' orientation. When you rotate attachment points in different directions, segments also rotate.

Color

The Color property tints the beam's texture to either a specific hue, or to a gradient ColorSequence across its entire span.

  1. In the Explorer window, select the beam.

  2. In the Properties window, select the Color property. You can either:

  3. Click on the color square to open the Colors pop-up window and select a color.

  4. Input three numbers into the RGB color value field.

  1. In the Explorer window, select the beam.
  2. In the Properties window, click inside the Color property field, then click the ⋯ button.

In the color sequence popup, each triangle on the bottom axis is a keypoint that determines the color value of the beam at that point along its span.

 <img src="../assets/studio/general/ColorSequence-White-Keypoints-Labeled.png" width="628" alt="Keypoints labeled in color sequence popup" />

  1. Click the keypoint at the start of the color sequence, click the small square next to Color, and select a color from the popup window.

  2. If you want the beam to change color near the end of its span, click the keypoint at the end of the color sequence, click the small square next to Color, and select a color from the popup window.

  1. For more customization, you can:

  2. Add another keypoint by clicking anywhere on the graph.

  3. Make a color change sooner or later within the gradient by dragging an intermediary keypoint to a new position.
  4. Delete an intermediary keypoint by selecting it and clicking the Delete button.
  5. Reset the entire sequence by clicking the Reset button.

Transparency

The Transparency property sets the transparency of the beam as a consistent value or as a NumberSequence with ranges from 0 (totally opaque) to 1 (fully clear).

  1. In the Explorer window, select the beam.
  2. In the Properties window, select the Transparency property.
  3. Input the desired opacity for the beam.
  1. In the Explorer window, select the beam.
  2. In the Properties window, click inside the Transparency property field, then click the ⋯ button.

In the number sequence popup, each square at the start and end of the graph is a keypoint that determines the opacity value of the beam at that point along its span. By default, the graph defaults to a straight line and the beam is of consistent opacity.

  1. Perform any of the following actions:

  2. To change the opacity at a point, click on a keypoint and either drag it up or down, or enter a value in the Value field.

  3. To insert a new keypoint, click on any point in the graph.
  4. To delete a keypoint, select it and click the Delete button.
  5. Reset the entire sequence by clicking the Reset button.

Width

You can set the beam's width in studs at each endpoint by configuring the Width0 and Width1 properties. A higher value equates to a larger width and a lower value equates to a smaller width. If you set either value to smaller than 0, Studio sets it back to 0.

The beam below has a Width0 value of 0.5 and a Width1 value of 3.

Texture length/mode

A beam's TextureLength and TextureMode determine how its texture repeats across its length.

When TextureMode is set to TextureMode.Wrap or TextureMode.Static, the texture repetitions will equal the beam's overall length (in studs) divided by its TextureLength.

Facing

A beam is a 2D projection existing in 3D space, meaning that it may not be visible from every angle. The FaceCamera property, when set to true, ensures that the beam always faces the CurrentCamera, regardless of its orientation.

Curve

Beams are configured to use a cubic Bézier curve formed by four control points. This means they are not constrained to straight lines and the curve of the beam can be modified by changing CurveSize0, CurveSize1, and the orientation of the beam's Attachments.

  • P0 — The start of the beam; position of Attachment0.
  • P1 — CurveSize0 studs away from Attachment0, in the positive X direction of Attachment0.
  • P2 — CurveSize1 studs away from Attachment1, in the negative X direction of Attachment1.
  • P3 — The end of the beam; position of Attachment1.

kid.simple: A `Beam` draws a picture stretched between two attachments, like a laser, rope of light, waterfall, or force field. You can color it, fade it, make it wider at one end, and even bend it into a curve. Beams are one of the easiest ways to make cool sci-fi or magic effects. The two attachments decide where it starts and ends.
kid.analogy: It is like a ribbon tied between two hooks: move the hooks and the ribbon moves with them, and you can choose the ribbon's pattern, color, and how wide each end is.
keyPoints: A beam needs two attachments: `Attachment0` is the start and `Attachment1` is the end. Remove one and the beam disappears.
To build one: put an attachment in each of two parts, insert a Beam, then set its `Attachment0` and `Attachment1` properties.
`Texture` sets the picture, `Color` tints it (one color or a gradient), and `Transparency` can fade it along its length.
`Width0` and `Width1` set how wide each end is in studs. Values below 0 are reset to 0.
`TextureLength` and `TextureMode` decide how often the texture repeats along the beam.
`FaceCamera = true` keeps the flat beam turned toward the camera so it does not vanish when seen from the side.
Beams can curve. `CurveSize0` and `CurveSize1` bend it, using each attachment's facing direction.
Turn on Show Constraint Details in the View menu to see attachments while building.

terms.attachment: An invisible point in a part that marks where something connects. Beams start at one attachment and end at another.
terms.texture: The image drawn along the beam, like a striped laser pattern.
terms.ColorSequence: A color gradient. A beam can go from blue at the start to purple at the end.
terms.NumberSequence: A list of numbers that change along the beam, used to fade transparency from 0 at one end to 1 at the other.
terms.opaque / transparent: Opaque (0) means you cannot see through it; fully transparent (1) means invisible.
terms.Width0 / Width1: How wide the beam is at the start and at the end. Width0 = 0.5 and Width1 = 3 makes it flare out like a cone.
terms.TextureMode: How the image repeats. With Wrap or Static, a 20-stud beam with TextureLength 4 repeats the image 5 times. With Stretch, it repeats exactly TextureLength times.
terms.segments: The little pieces a beam is split into so it can bend smoothly. More segments make a smoother curve.
terms.Bezier curve: A smooth curve shaped by control points. The beam bends toward points that sit `CurveSize0` studs out from the start and `CurveSize1` studs out from the end.
terms.2D projection: Something flat drawn in a 3D world. Seen exactly edge-on, it can look invisible.

example.title: Draw a glowing laser between two parts
example.place: Script in ServerScriptService (with two parts named LaserStart and LaserEnd in Workspace)
example.code:
local startPart = workspace:WaitForChild("LaserStart")
local endPart = workspace:WaitForChild("LaserEnd")

local attach0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
attach0.Parent = startPart
local attach1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
attach1.Parent = endPart

local beam = Instance.new("Beam")
beam.Attachment0 = attach0
beam.Attachment1 = attach1
beam.Color = ColorSequence.new(Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0))
beam.Width0 = 0.3
beam.Width1 = 0.3
beam.FaceCamera = true -- always visible from any angle
beam.LightEmission = 1 -- glow
beam.Parent = startPart
explain: We find the two parts and add an attachment to each one.
We create a `Beam` and tell it which attachment is the start and which is the end.
We make it red and 0.3 studs wide at both ends.
`FaceCamera` keeps it from disappearing when viewed from the side.
Parenting it into the game makes it show up. Move either part and the beam follows.

watchOut: Setting both attachments to the same attachment draws nothing. They must be two different attachments.
If your beam vanishes at certain angles, turn on `FaceCamera`.
A beam that is unexpectedly curved probably has nonzero `CurveSize0` or `CurveSize1`. Set them to 0 for a straight line.
A beam is just a picture. It does not block or hurt players unless you script that.
